plugin.title: Plugins
plugin.shot_timeline_hint: *The annotations are created based on the shot boundaries of the selected timeline
plugin.scalar_timeline_hint: *The scalar values of the selected timelines will be aggregated

active_speaker_detection.plugin_description: This plugin does active speaker detection based on audio and tracked face data.

aggregation.plugin_description:
This plugin allows you to combine information from multiple timelines with logical operators. In this way, more complex patterns can be revealed. For example, the logical and can be used to detect when two concepts or persons are visible simultaneously.

Tip: You can perform the plugin multiple times to create more complex patterns. The following example performs three aggregations to detect when a Concept A is simultaneously visible with Concept B or Concept C:

AGG1 = (Concept A) Logical And (Concept B)
AGG2 = (Concept A) Logical And (Concept C)
AGG3 = (AGG1) Logical Or (AGG2)

Parameters

  • Timelines to combine: two or more timelines with scalar values (e.g., probabilities). Timelines with annotations, such as shots or transcripts, cannot be combined.
  • Aggregation Method: how the values are combined.

audio_classification.plugin_description:
This plugin recognizes which kinds of sounds occur in each shot of the video, for example speech, laughter, music genres, musical instruments, animals, vehicles, or explosions. It uses the EAT (Efficient Audio Transformer) model, trained on Google's AudioSet dataset, which distinguishes 527 sound classes (list as CSV file).

The result is a timeline with one segment per shot, labeled with the recognized sound classes (English AudioSet names). Several classes can be recognized at the same time, for example speech and background music. Shots in which no class reaches the confidence threshold remain without a label.

Note: Currently, onle the first 10 seconds of each shots are analyzed. We are working on a solution.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the timeline whose shots are analyzed, e.g., the result of the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin.
  • Number of predicted classes (top-k): the maximum number of sound classes per shot. Higher values allow more labels per shot.
  • Confidence threshold: the minimum probability a sound class needs to be shown. Higher values show fewer but more reliable labels; lower values also show uncertain ones.

audio_emotion.plugin_description: This plugin detects emotions from audio segments (retrieved with WhisperX).

audio_frequency.plugin_description:
This plugin shows which frequencies are present in the audio track over time. The librosa library computes a short-time Fourier transform (STFT): the audio is split into short, overlapping windows, and the strength of each frequency is measured within each window. The result is displayed as a heatmap, with time on the horizontal axis and frequency on the vertical axis, from low at the bottom to high at the top.

The spectrogram can reveal voices, music, rhythmic patterns, and other recurring sounds. Intensities are scaled from 0 (weakest) to 1 (strongest in the video), so they are best compared within one video rather than between videos.

Parameters

  • Sampling rate: the highest frequency shown is half the sampling rate. Higher values show more detail in music and noises but take longer to compute.
  • FFT window length (samples): longer windows separate neighboring frequencies more finely but blur short sounds in time; shorter windows show short sounds more precisely but with coarser frequencies.

audio_gender.plugin_description: This plugin detects the gender from audio/speech segments (retrieved with WhisperX).

audio_rms.plugin_description:
This plugin measures how loud the audio track is over time. The librosa library computes the root mean square (RMS) energy of the audio in short, overlapping windows.

The timeline reveals silent passages, loud scenes such as music or action sequences, and sudden changes in volume. The curve is scaled from 0 (the quietest moment of the video) to 1 (the loudest), so it is best used to compare passages within one video rather than between videos.

Parameters

  • Sampling rate: higher values give a finer time resolution but take longer to compute.

audio_waveform.plugin_description:
This plugin draws the waveform of the audio track, similar to the view in an audio editor. The librosa library resamples the audio to a fixed number of points so that it can be displayed as a timeline.

Silence lies around the middle of the timeline; the further the curve swings up and down, the louder the sound. The scale is relative to the quietest and loudest values of the video, so the waveform is best compared within one video. To follow the volume over time, the "Audio Volume (RMS)" plugin is easier to read.

Parameters

  • Sampling rate: the rate at which the audio is loaded. Higher values keep more detail but take longer to compute.

blip.plugin_description:
This plugin uses the large vision language model InstructBLIP that is similar to GPT-4 to perform question answering over the video. It can be used for various purposes, for example, to automatically find concepts within the video. Here are some examples:

Does this image show a car? Please answer with yes or no!
Does this image show at least three persons? Please answer with yes or no!
Is this photo taken in a restaurant? Please answer with yes or no!

clip.plugin_description:
This plugin searches the video for any visual concept you describe in words, e.g., objects, places, situations, times of day, or weather conditions. It uses a multilingual OpenCLIP model (model details) trained by LAION on billions of image–text pairs, based on the CLIP architecture by Radford et al. (2021).

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and CLIP compares each frame with your description. To make the comparison more robust, the description is automatically inserted into 80 standard phrasings such as "a photo of a …" or "a drawing of a …", and the results are averaged. The timeline shows for each moment how well the frame matches the description.

The values are scaled per timeline, so the best-matching moment is always 1, even if the concept does not appear in the video at all. Read the timeline as "where the concept most likely appears", not as a yes/no answer.

CLIP works well for concepts that can be recognized in a single frame. For concepts that require movement over time, such as human actions, use the "Action Classification (X-CLIP)" plugin.

Parameters

  • Concept Description: the concept you are looking for, in simple, unambiguous terms, e.g., car, a red car, or people dancing in the rain. Do not add phrases like "a photo of", because they are added automatically. Descriptions in other languages work as well, but English usually gives the best results.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values also find concepts that are only visible briefly, but take longer to compute.

clip_ontology.plugin_name: Visual Concept Classification with a Concept List (CLIP)
clip_ontology.plugin_description:
This plugin assigns the frames of the video to a list of visual concepts that you define, e.g., times of day, places, or types of scenes. It uses the same multilingual OpenCLIP model (model details) trained by LAION as the "Visual Concept Search (CLIP)" plugin.

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and CLIP compares each frame with the descriptions of all concepts in your list. The similarities are converted into probabilities that add up to 1 for each frame. Each frame is therefore always assigned to the concepts in your list, even if none of them fits. Your list should therefore cover all alternatives that can occur, e.g., day and night, or indoor and outdoor. To search for a single concept on its own, use the "Visual Concept Search (CLIP)" plugin instead.

The result consists of one timeline per concept, showing its probability over time. If a shot timeline is selected, an additional timeline labels each shot with the concept that has the highest average probability within the shot.

CLIP works well for concepts that can be recognized in a single frame. For concepts that require movement over time, such as human actions, use the "Action Classification (X-CLIP)" plugin.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: optional. If a shot timeline is selected, each shot is labeled with its most likely concept.

  • Concept Lexicon: a CSV file with one concept per row and two columns separated by commas: the name of the concept, which is used as the name of its timeline, and a description in simple, unambiguous terms. Unlike in "Visual Concept Search (CLIP)", the descriptions are used exactly as written, so full phrases work best. Do not include a header row. Example:

    "day","a photo taken at daylight"
    "night","a photo taken during the night"

    If you create the file with a spreadsheet program, make sure it is saved with commas, not semicolons.

  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values also find concepts that are only visible briefly, but take longer to compute.
clip_ontology.concepts_hint: CSV file with one concept per row; first column the name, second column a description

color_analysis.plugin_description:
This plugin determines the dominant colors of the video over time. Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate and scaled down to the selected maximum resolution. For each frame, the colors of all pixels are grouped with the k-means clustering algorithm of the scikit-learn library into the selected number of groups. The average color of each group is one dominant color, and the groups are ranked by how many pixels they contain.

The result is shown as color timelines. With one color, a single timeline shows it; with several colors, a group contains one timeline per rank, where "#0" is the color covering the largest area of the frame, "#1" the second largest, and so on.

Parameters

  • Number of dominant color(s): how many colors are determined per frame; each color gets its own timeline. Higher values also show secondary colors.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values show color changes more precisely in time but take longer to compute.
  • Maximum Image Resolution (advanced option): the size, in pixels, of the longer side of the frames after scaling down. Higher values let small areas count more precisely but take longer to compute; since dominant colors cover large areas, low values are usually sufficient.
  • Maximum Number of Iterations for k-Means Clustering (advanced option): how many refinement steps the clustering may take per frame. Higher values can group the colors slightly more precisely but take longer to compute; this value rarely needs to be changed.
color_analysis.max_resolution: Maximum image resolution used for the analysis
color_analysis.max_iter: Maximum number of iterations for k-Means clustering

color_brightness_analysis.plugin_description:
This plugin measures how bright the video is over time. Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate and converted to the HSV color model with the OpenCV library. The brightness of a frame is the average "value" (V) of all its pixels, where 0 is black and 1 is the maximum brightness. The timeline can reveal dark and bright scenes, for example night and day scenes, as well as fades and lighting changes.

Parameters

  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values show brightness changes more precisely in time but take longer to compute.
  • Normalize Results? (advanced option): if enabled, the curve is scaled so that the darkest frame of the video is 0 and the brightest is 1. This makes differences within a video easier to see, but the values can no longer be compared between videos. If disabled, the absolute values are shown, which can be compared between videos.

face_clustering.plugin_description:
This plugin gives you an overview of the main characters in the video by grouping their faces into clusters, ideally one cluster per person. It is not meant to find every appearance of a person; that is done in a second step (see below).

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and faces are detected with the SCRFD face detector of InsightFace. Faces smaller than the selected minimum height are discarded: small faces are often blurry and would make the clusters less stable. For each remaining face, an ArcFace model computes a numerical description of the facial features, and faces with similar features are grouped into clusters. Two faces end up in the same cluster if they are similar enough, either directly or through a chain of similar faces. Because of this chaining, a threshold that is only slightly too high can merge different people into one cluster.

Typical workflow

  1. Create clusters: run this plugin and check the clusters in the tab "Faces". Each main character relevant for your analysis should have one cluster that contains only this person. Remove wrong faces or merge clusters where needed, or run the plugin again with a different threshold.
  2. Convert clusters to timelines: for each relevant cluster, create a timeline in the tab "Faces". The average of the cluster's sample faces is used as a reference for the person, and all faces in the video are compared with it. The timeline shows for each moment how similar the most similar face is to the reference. The values are scaled per timeline, so the highest value is always 1: read the timeline as "where the person most likely appears", not as a yes/no answer.
  3. Visualize relations: use the visualization options of TIB-AV-A to create a constellation graph that shows which persons appear together.

The persons are not identified by name, but you can manually provide names in step 2.

Parameters

  • Clustering threshold: how different two faces may be and still belong to the same cluster. Lower values create more and purer clusters, but one person may be split into several clusters. Higher values create fewer clusters, but different people may be merged.
  • Maximum number of clusters: how many of the largest clusters are kept. Smaller clusters, often minor characters or false detections, are discarded.
  • Sample faces per cluster: how many face images of each cluster are shown in the tab "Faces". These sample faces are also the reference when a cluster is converted to a timeline: more samples make the reference more robust, provided they all show the same person.
  • Minimum face height: the minimum height of a face as a fraction of the frame height. Higher values keep only larger, sharper faces and make the clusters more stable; lower values also include people in the background, but blurry faces can mix up the clusters. Small faces are still taken into account when a cluster is converted to a timeline.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are searched for faces. Higher values find more faces, including people who are only visible briefly, but take longer to compute.

Tip: if a cluster contains several people, lower the clustering threshold. If one person is spread over several clusters, raise it slightly or merge the clusters in the tab "Faces".
face_clustering.clustering_method_hint: Both methods currently produce the same result.

face_identification.plugin_description:
This plugin searches the video for a person shown in an example image you upload, and creates a timeline showing where this person most likely appears. It is useful if you already have a photo of the person. To get an overview of the main characters without a photo, use the "Face Clustering" plugin instead.

The face in the example image and all faces in the video are detected with the SCRFD face detector of InsightFace. For each face, an ArcFace model computes a numerical description of the facial features. Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and every face in a frame is compared with the example face. For each moment, the timeline shows how similar the most similar face is.

The values are scaled per timeline, so the highest value is always 1, even if the person does not appear in the video at all. Read the timeline as "where the person most likely appears", not as a yes/no answer.

Parameters

  • Example image: a photo of the person you are looking for, as JPG, PNG, or WebP file. The face should be clearly and entirely visible, in good resolution, and the image should show only this person: if it contains several faces, all of them are searched for. If no face is found in the image, the plugin fails.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are searched. Higher values also find people who are only visible briefly, but take longer to compute.
face_identification.query_images_hint: The image should show only the person you are looking for, with the face clearly visible and in good quality.

faceemotion.plugin_description:
This plugin recognizes the facial expressions of the people in the video. Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and faces are detected with the SCRFD face detector of InsightFace. Since facial expressions should be clearly visible, use the parameter "minimum face size" to discard small faces. Each face is then classified with the facial expression model of DeepFace into seven classes (cf. Ekman): angry, disgust, fear, happy, sad, surprise, and neutral.

The result consists of one timeline per expression, showing its probability over time. If several faces are visible at the same time, their probabilities are combined, so in scenes with many faces all expressions can receive high values. If a shot timeline is selected, an additional timeline labels each shot with the expression that has the highest average probability within the shot.

Results are most reliable for frontal, large, and well-lit faces with clear expressions; subtle expressions are often classified as neutral or confused with each other.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: If a shot timeline is selected, each shot is labeled with its most likely expression; without it, only the probability timelines are created.
  • Minimum face height: the minimum height of a face as a fraction of the frame height. Facial expressions can only be recognized in sufficiently large faces, so higher values give more reliable results; lower values also include people in the background, whose expressions are often misclassified.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values also capture short expressions but take longer to compute.

invert.plugin_description:
This plugin inverts a timeline with values: high values become low and low values become high. Each value is replaced by 1 minus the value; values outside the range from 0 to 1 are first scaled to this range.

Together with the "Combine Timelines" plugin, it can be used to find moments when something is not the case. For example, to find when person A is visible but person B is not:

INV = Invert (Person B)
RESULT = (Person A) Logical And (INV)

Parameters

  • Timeline to invert: the timeline with values to be inverted, e.g., a person timeline or the result of "Single-Object Classification (CLIP)".

movie_pattern_frameshare.plugin_description: This plugin detects the movie pattern frameshare based on the shot boundaries of a selected timeline.
movie_pattern_frameshare.min_length: Minimum Length of the Pattern in Shots

movie_pattern_intensify.plugin_description: This plugin detects the movie pattern intensification based on the shot boundaries of a selected timeline.
movie_pattern_intensify.min_length: Minimum Length of the Pattern in Shots

movie_pattern_opposition.plugin_description: This plugin detects the movie pattern opposition based on the shot boundaries of a selected timeline.
movie_pattern_opposition.min_length: Minimum Length of the Pattern in Shots

movie_pattern_shot_reverse_shot.plugin_description: This plugin detects the movie pattern shot reverse shot based on the shot boundaries of a selected timeline.
movie_pattern_shot_reverse_shot.min_length: Minimum Length of the Pattern in Shots

place_clustering.plugin_description:
This plugin gives you an overview of the recurring settings in the video by grouping shots that show the same or a very similar place, e.g., the same apartment, office, or street. Unlike "Place Recognition (Places365)", which assigns general categories such as "kitchen", it finds places that occur several times in this particular video.

For each shot of the selected shot timeline, the middle frame is used. A multilingual OpenCLIP model computes a numerical description of each image, and images with similar descriptions are grouped into clusters, ideally one cluster per place. Two shots end up in the same cluster if they are similar enough, either directly or through a chain of similar shots. Because of this chaining, a threshold that is only slightly too high can merge different places into one cluster.

Please note that the comparison is based on how similar the images look. Two different places that look alike, e.g., two kitchens, can end up in the same cluster, and the same place shown from very different angles can be split into several clusters.

Typical workflow

  1. Create clusters: run this plugin and check the clusters in the tab "Places". Remove wrong images or merge clusters where needed, or run the plugin again with a different threshold.
  2. Convert clusters to timelines: for each relevant cluster, create a timeline in the tab "Places" to see when the place appears in the video.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be grouped, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. One image per shot is used, so the quality of the shot timeline directly determines the result.
  • Clustering threshold: how different two images may be and still belong to the same cluster. Lower values create more and purer clusters, but one place may be split into several clusters. Higher values create fewer clusters, but different places may be merged.
  • Maximum number of clusters: how many of the largest clusters are kept. Smaller clusters, often places that appear only once, are discarded.

Tip: if a cluster contains different places, lower the clustering threshold. If one place is spread over several clusters, raise it slightly or merge the clusters in the tab "Places".
place_clustering.clustering_method_hint: Both methods currently produce the same result.

places_classification.plugin_description:
This plugin recognizes the type of place shown in each shot, e.g., a kitchen, a street, a forest, or a church. It uses a ResNet-50 network trained on the Places365 dataset of about 1.8 million place (or scene) images. Places are recognized on three levels of detail:

  • 3 categories: indoor, outdoor natural, and outdoor man-made
  • 16 categories: e.g., home or hotel, transportation, forest or field
  • 365 categories: e.g., kitchen, bus station, bamboo forest

The full list of categories and how they are grouped can be found here.

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and the model estimates for each frame how likely each of the 365 categories is; the probabilities of the coarser levels are derived from them. Each shot of the selected shot timeline is then labeled with the most likely place on each of the three levels on average across the shot.

The result is a timeline with three labels per shot, one for each level, together with one timeline for each of the three top-level categories that shows its probability over time.

Please note that the model recognizes the type of a place, not a specific location: it can tell that a scene shows a church, but not which church. To group shots that show the same location, use the "Place Clustering" plugin.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be labeled, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. Its quality determines the result, so check it for missed or false cuts first.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values capture changes of the place within a shot more precisely but take longer to compute.

shot_angle.plugin_description:
This plugin determines the camera angle of each shot, i.e., from which direction the camera looks at the scene. It uses a ConvNeXt V2 image classifier that we trained on the camera angle annotations of the CineScale dataset of feature films. It distinguishes five camera angles:

  • Overhead: the camera looks straight down from above (bird's-eye view)
  • High: the camera is above the subject and looks down at it
  • Neutral: the camera is at about the height of the subject and looks straight at it
  • Low: the camera is below the subject and looks up at it
  • Dutch: the camera is tilted sideways, so that the horizon is slanted

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and the model estimates for each frame how likely each camera angle is. Each shot of the selected shot timeline is then labeled with the camera angle that is the most likely on average across the shot.

The result is a timeline with one camera angle per shot, together with one timeline per camera angle that shows its probability over time.

Please note that each frame is assigned exactly one camera angle. A shot that is both tilted sideways and taken from above is therefore labeled either "Dutch" or "High". The model analyzes a square section from the center of each frame, so details at the left and right edges of widescreen images are not taken into account.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be labeled, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. Its quality determines the result, so check it for missed or false cuts first.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values capture changes of the camera angle within a shot more precisely but take longer to compute.

shot_density.plugin_description:
This plugin shows how fast the video is edited over time, i.e., how closely the cuts follow each other. It uses the shot boundaries of a selected timeline, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. The kernel density estimation of the scikit-learn library places a bell-shaped curve on each cut and adds these curves up. Where many cuts follow each other closely, the curve is high; during long shots, it is low.

The result is a timeline that distinguishes fast-paced passages, such as action sequences or montages, from slow-paced ones. The values are scaled from 0 (slowest editing in the video) to 1 (fastest), so they are relative to the video and cannot be compared between videos.

shot_detection.plugin_description:
This plugin automatically splits the video into shots. It uses TransNet V2, a neural network trained to recognize both hard cuts and gradual transitions such as dissolves and fades. Every frame of the video is analyzed, and the network estimates for each frame how likely a shot transition takes place.

The result is a timeline with one segment per shot. Many other plugins use this timeline as input, for example to annotate shots or compute the shot density. Mistakes can be corrected directly on the timeline: right-click a shot to split it at the current position or to merge it with its neighbors.

Please note that very fast camera movements, flashes, or sudden lighting changes can occasionally be mistaken for cuts, and very soft transitions can be missed.

shot_level.plugin_description:
This plugin determines the camera level of each shot, i.e., at which height the camera is placed relative to the subject. It uses a ConvNeXt V2 image classifier that we trained on the camera level annotations of the CineScale dataset of feature films. It distinguishes six camera levels:

  • Aerial: the camera is high above the scene, e.g., on a crane, helicopter, or drone
  • Eye: the camera is at the eye level of the people in the scene
  • Shoulder: the camera is at about shoulder height
  • Hip: the camera is at about hip height
  • Knee: the camera is at about knee height
  • Ground: the camera is placed on or close to the ground

The camera level describes where the camera is, not in which direction it looks. Use the "Camera Angle Classification" plugin to determine whether the camera looks up, down, or straight ahead.

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and the model estimates for each frame how likely each camera level is. Each shot of the selected shot timeline is then labeled with the camera level that is the most likely on average across the shot.

The result is a timeline with one camera level per shot, together with one timeline per camera level that shows its probability over time.

Please note that the camera level is defined relative to the people in the scene. For shots without people, it is estimated from the surroundings, which is less reliable. The model analyzes a square section from the center of each frame, so details at the left and right edges of widescreen images are not taken into account.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be labeled, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. Its quality determines the result, so check it for missed or false cuts first.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values capture changes of the camera level within a shot more precisely but take longer to compute.

shot_scalar_annotation.plugin_description:
This plugin converts a timeline with scalar values (e.g., probabilities) into shot annotations. For each shot of the selected shot timeline, the average of the values within the shot is computed. The result is a new timeline with one segment per shot, labeled with the average value. The color of each segment indicates the value compared with the other shots: the higher the value, the brighter the color.

Shot annotations can be compared shot by shot and exported together with the other annotations, e.g., to ELAN for further analysis. Shots that are shorter than the time step of the selected curve contain no value and remain without a segment.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots for which the averages are computed, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin.
  • Timeline with values: the timeline whose curve is averaged per shot.

shot_scale_and_movement.plugin_description:
This plugin classifies both the shot scale and the camera movement of each shot. It uses a VideoMAE video transformer that we trained on the MovieShots dataset of shots from movie trailers. Unlike classifiers that look at single frames, it analyzes short video sections and can therefore recognize camera movements.

The model distinguishes five shot scales:

  • Extreme Close-Up: only a small detail fills the frame, e.g., the eyes of a person or a part of an object
  • Close-Up: a face, a hand, or a small object fills most of the frame
  • Medium: a person from about the waist up, or a subject seen at a similar distance
  • Full: a person from head to toe, or a subject that is entirely visible and fills the frame
  • Long: people or objects appear small in their surroundings, e.g., landscapes or wide views of a scene

and four types of camera movement:

  • Static: the camera does not move
  • Motion: the camera moves, e.g., pans, tilts, or follows a subject
  • Push: the camera moves toward the subject or zooms in
  • Pull: the camera moves away from the subject or zooms out

The video is split into sections of half a second, and the model estimates for each section how likely each class is. Each shot of the selected shot timeline is then labeled with the most likely scale and the most likely movement on average across the shot.

The result consists of two groups of timelines, one for the shot scale and one for the camera movement. Each group contains a timeline with one label per shot and one timeline per class showing its probability over time.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be labeled, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. Its quality determines the result, so check it for missed or false cuts first.

shot_type_classification.plugin_description:
This plugin determines the shot scale (or shot size) of each shot, i.e., how large the people or objects appear in the frame. A neural network (ResNet) classifies frames of the video into five shot sizes, i.e., Extreme Close-Up, Close-Up, Medium Shot, Full Shot, and Long Shot.

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate, and the network estimates for each frame how likely each shot size is. Each shot of the selected shot timeline is then labeled with the shot size that is the most likely on average across the shot. If the shot size changes within a shot, e.g., because of a zoom or camera movement, the label shows the size that dominates on average; the probability timelines show the changes in detail.

The result is a timeline with one shot size per shot, together with one timeline per shot size that shows its probability over time.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be labeled, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. Its quality determines the result, so check it for missed or false cuts first.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are analyzed. Higher values capture changes in shot size within a shot more precisely but take longer to compute.

text_ner.plugin_description: This plugin performs Named Entity Recognition (NER) and subsequently Entity Linking / Disambiguation based on the speaker segments of WhisperX.

text_pos.plugin_description: This plugin performs PoS Tagging based on the speaker segments of WhisperX. For each speaker segment the count of each PoS-Tag is shown.

text_sentiment.plugin_description: This plugin performs sentiment analysis based on the speaker segments of WhisperX. The predicted label is shown as well as the predicted probabilities for each sentiment.

thumbnail.plugin_description:
This plugin creates small preview images of the video. They are used in the tab "Shots", which shows three thumbnails for each shot: one from the beginning, one from the middle, and one from the end.

The plugin runs automatically when a video is uploaded, so you normally do not need to start it yourself. Run it again only if the thumbnails in the tab "Shots" are missing, e.g., because the automatic run failed. If it has been run several times, the most recent thumbnails are used.

vllm.plugin_description:
This plugin lets you ask a question about every shot of the video, or give an instruction such as "Describe the image", and stores the answer of a generative large vision-language model as an annotation of the shot. It uses Google's Gemma 4 model, which understands both images and text and runs locally at an Ollama instance at TIB. Thus, the images are not sent to an external service.

For each shot of the selected shot timeline, the frame in the middle of the shot is sent to the model together with your prompt. The answer is stored as the label of the shot. The same prompt on the same video always gives the same answers.

The result is a timeline with one segment per shot, labeled with the model's answer. With prompts that ask for short, fixed answers, the timeline can be used like a classification, for example:

Is there a car in this image? Answer only with yes or no.
How many people are visible? Answer only with a number.
Is this scene indoors or outdoors? Answer with one word.

Please note that the model only sees one frame per shot, so it cannot answer questions about what happens over the course of a shot. Like all language models, it can give wrong answers that sound convincing, so check important results against the video.

Parameters

  • Shot Boundaries from Timeline: the shots to be analyzed, e.g., the timeline created by the "Shot Boundary Detection" plugin. One frame per shot is used.
  • Query / Prompt: the question or instruction for the model. Ask for short answers, e.g., "Answer only with yes or no", because the complete answer becomes the label of the shot; very long answers are shortened. The prompt can be written in other languages as well.

whisper.plugin_description:
This plugin transcribes the speech in the video with OpenAI's Whisper model (paper). Whisper detects the spoken language automatically and supports about 100 languages. The transcript is split into short phrases with their start and end times.

The transcript is shown as a timeline and in the tab "Transcript", where you can search for words. The tab "Word Cloud" shows the most frequent words.

The plugin does not distinguish between speakers. Please use "Speech & Speaker Recognition (WhisperX)" for that. Whisper can occasionally produce text for music, noise, or silence, so check important passages against the video.

whisper_x.plugin_description:
This plugin transcribes the speech in the video and determines who speaks when. It uses WhisperX, which combines three steps:

  1. Speech recognition: OpenAI's Whisper model (large-v3) transcribes the audio. Passages without speech are skipped, which reduces invented text during music or silence.
  2. Word alignment: a wav2vec 2.0 model aligns every word precisely with the audio.
  3. Speaker diarization: pyannote.audio groups similar voices into speakers and assigns each phrase to one speaker.

The result is a group of two timelines: "Speech Transcript" contains each phrase with its speaker, and "Speaker" shows when each speaker talks. Speakers are numbered (SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01, …) separately for each video; they are not identified by name.

Parameters

  • Language Code: the spoken language as a two-letter code, e.g., en or de. Keep none to detect it automatically. Entering it is more reliable for short videos or videos with a lot of music. It supports the 41 languages with a WhisperX alignment model.
  • Speaker clustering threshold: how similar two voices must be to count as the same speaker. Lower values produce more speakers, higher values fewer.
  • Speaker regularization (Fb): how strongly a small number of speakers is preferred. Higher values produce fewer speakers.
  • Acoustic scaling (Fa): how much small differences between voices count. Higher values tend to produce more speakers.
whisper_x.language_code_hint: If not provided, the spoken language is detected automatically

x_clip.plugin_description:
This plugin searches the video for visual concepts and actions you describe in words, e.g., people dancing, a person playing guitar, or someone running. It uses X-CLIP, a video version of CLIP that analyzes short video clips instead of single frames, and can therefore recognize what happens over time. The model was trained on the Kinetics dataset of human actions and works best for everyday and sports activities.

Frames are taken from the video at the selected rate and grouped into clips of eight frames. X-CLIP compares each clip with your description, and the timeline shows for each clip how well it matches.

The values are scaled per timeline, so the best-matching clip is always 1, even if the action does not occur in the video at all. Read the timeline as "where the action most likely happens", not as a yes/no answer.

For concepts that can be recognized in a single frame, such as objects or places, the "Visual Concept Search (CLIP)" plugin is usually more precise.

Parameters

  • Action Description: the action you are looking for, in English and in simple, unambiguous terms, e.g., people dancing or a person riding a bicycle. Short descriptions of the activity usually work best.
  • Frames per Second (FPS) (advanced option): how many frames per second are used. Because each clip always consists of eight frames, this value also determines how long each clip is: lower values give longer clips, which suit slow or long actions; higher values give shorter clips with a finer time resolution, but longer actions may then be split into fragments.

welcome.title: TIB AV-Analytics
welcome.text: Welcome to the TIB AV-Analytics (TIB-AV-A) video analysis platform for systematic film and video analysis.
welcome.login_text:
If you do not have an account yet, you can create an account at the top right ("Login" -> "Register").
New users can upload a maximum number of ten videos with a maximum file size of 500 MB.

If you have questions regarding account creation or if you want to analyze more or larger video files, please write an email to matthias.springstein@tib.eu with a short explanation of your intended use case
welcome.format_text: Please note that TIB-AV-A currently only supports the analysis of mp4 video files to avoid long processing times due to transcoding videos on our server. Please transcode them before uploading. If you have questions, feel free to contact us: matthias.springstein@tib.eu
